title: A fatherly household
hookLine: from Sextus: kindness, dignity without show, and patience with the unlearned (Meditations 1.9)

cards: Someone at work asks the question everyone else learned years ago. Where's the shared drive? What does that acronym mean?
A sigh is right there, ready to be given. Anyone who has been new somewhere has heard that sigh from the other side.
Book one's ninth entry is about a teacher who never gave it: a philosopher with a well-known family name, and a whole house with a certain feel to it.

teach.b: First, Sextus. A philosopher from Chaeronea in Greece, and, ancient writers say, a relative of the writer Plutarch, perhaps his nephew. Marcus studied with him.
Second, the household. From Sextus, Marcus says, he learned kindness, and saw the example of a family governed in a fatherly way. Living by nature.
Dignity without putting it on. Watching out for his friends' interests. Company so easy that it was more pleasant than any flattery, while everyone still respected him.
Sextus was free of anger, Marcus says, and yet full of affection. Calm didn't make him cold. Third, the patience.
Marcus learned from him to put up with people who don't know things, and with people who form opinions without thinking them through. Not to sneer, not to sigh, just to bear with them.
At home, that's the parent who explains again.

teach.h: A HOUSE RUN LIKE A FATHER'S.
teach.b: In school, it's the teacher who hears the same question for the twentieth time and answers it like the first. Fourth, the emperor goes to school.
A later writer, Philostratus, tells a story that even as emperor, Marcus kept going to hear Sextus lecture.

teach.h: BEAR WITH THOSE WHO DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: Asked where he was going, Marcus answered, roughly, that it's good even for an older man to learn, and he was off to Sextus to learn what he didn't yet know.
Whether every word is accurate or not, it fits.
It's easier to be patient with beginners when you never stop being one.

how: Readers who take this entry to heart often practice answering beginners' questions without impatience, and keep learning something new themselves.

o: the Greek writer Plutarch, under a Latin pen name
the teacher who showed Marcus patience and calm kindness
the sixth emperor of Rome, who ruled long before Marcus

Marcus says he was free of anger and yet full of affection.

and with people who simply don't know.

games.q: you're the emperor of Rome, and someone asks why you're still going to a philosopher's lectures. what do you say?
o: an emperor has nothing left to learn.
it's good even for an older man to learn what he doesn't know.
games.why: in Philostratus' story, Marcus says he's going to Sextus to learn what he doesn't yet know.

practice: Think of someone who often doesn't know what you know, a new coworker, an older parent with a phone, a child asking why again, and notice the sigh rising as they ask.
Picture answering the way Sextus might have: plainly, warmly, as if no one had asked before. Then remember one thing you're a beginner at yourself.

wordCard.voice: Sextus. The philosopher from whom Marcus learned kindness without show, calm without coldness, and patience with people who don't yet know. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: full of natural affection, the warmth Marcus saw in Sextus alongside his calm.

carryVoice: Your line: patient with the unlearned. Everyone is a beginner at something, even an emperor. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Lives of the Sophists 2.1 (Marcus and Sextus)
